english_translation: The road had potholes, but the journey went well without any problem.

dialogue.shona: Mugwagwa wangauine makomba asi rwendo rwazofamba zvakanaka; pasina dambudziko.
dialogue.english: The road had potholes, but the journey went well without any problem.
dialogue.literal_gloss: Mugwagwa [in / singular gwagwa] • wangauine [wangauine] • makomba [plural komba] • asi [but / however] • rwendo [rwendo] • rwazofamba [rwazofamba] • zvakanaka [well / nicely / very good] • pasina [on / at sina] • dambudziko [dambudziko]

grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'zvakanaka' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: The Passive Voice ('-wa' / '-iwa') in 'Mugwagwa'
grammar_notes.content: Notice how 'Mugwagwa' ends in '-wa' right before the final '-a'. In Shona, you turn an active verb into a passive verb ('is done / was done')  simply by inserting '-w-' (or '-iw-' / '-ew-') before the final vowel '-a'! For example: '-bika' (cook) becomes '-bikwa' ('be cooked', as in 'pakubikwa'), '-vaka' (build) becomes '-vakwa' ('be built'), '-ruma' (bite/sting) becomes '-rumwa' ('be stung', as in 'arumwa nenyuchi'), and '-zivikanwa' means 'be known'.

grammar_notes.title: Describing How Actions Are Done: Adverbs & Intensifiers ('zvakanaka')
grammar_notes.content: To describe HOW an action is performed, Shona frequently uses the prefix 'zva-' / 'zvi-' or intensifiers like 'zvakanaka'. Compare these high-frequency expressions you will hear every day: 'zvakanaka' ('well / nicely'), 'zvakasimba' ('firmly / strongly'), 'zvishoma' ('a little bit'), 'zvinyoronyoro' ('gently / softly'), and 'chaizvo' or 'zvikuru' ('very much / davvero').
grammar_notes.rule: Verb + Adverb of Manner/Degree (zvakanaka = well, zvakasimba = firmly, zvishoma = a little, chaizvo/zvikuru = very much)

cultural_notes.title: Navigating Rainy-Season Road Potholes ('Makomba') Safely
cultural_notes.content: After heavy summer rains, drivers watch carefully for potholes ('makomba') along rural and suburban roads, celebrating a smooth, incident-free arrival ('rwendo rwazofamba zvakanaka; pasina dambudziko').

active_exercises.prompt: What does 'parutivi pemugwagwa' mean in 'Rori yakamira parutivi pemugwagwa'?
options: In the middle of the intersection
Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.correct_answer: Beside the road / on the side of the road
active_exercises.explanation: 'Parutivi pe-' means 'beside / at the side of', and 'mugwagwa' is 'road'.

active_exercises.prompt: How do you say 'Our journey was very good' in Shona?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Rwendo rwedu' = 'Our journey' (taking 'rw-' agreement), 'rwakanga rwakanaka kwazvo' = 'was very good'.

active_exercises.prompt: Why is 'white' written as 'chena' in 'hembe chena' (white shirt), but 'machena' in 'mabhuku machena' (white books)?
options: 'Machena' means light grey while 'chena' means bright white
Only clothing can use the word 'chena'
'Machena' is only used in the past tense
Colour adjectives change their prefix to match the noun they describe ('ma-' for 'mabhuku')
active_exercises.correct_answer: Colour adjectives change their prefix to match the noun they describe ('ma-' for 'mabhuku')
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, traditional colour stems (-chena, -tema, -tsvuku) take the prefix of the noun they describe.
